Table of Shewbread
TAY-bul uv SHOH-bred
n. phr. (the table in the holy place bearing the bread of the presence)
English shewbread, Tyndale's rendering of Hebrew lechem ha-panim, the bread of the face or presence; with table, Hebrew shulchan. The table is the article of furniture; the shewbread is what lay upon it.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The phrase occurs once in the Authorized Version, in the instructions for breaking camp: “And upon the table of shewbread they shall spread a cloth of blue, and put thereon the dishes, and the spoons, and the bowls, and covers to cover withal: and the continual bread shall be thereon.” The table stood in the holy place on the north side, over against the candlestick, and was made of shittim wood overlaid with gold, two cubits long, a cubit broad, and a cubit and a half high. Upon it were set twelve cakes of fine flour, “in two rows, six on a row, upon the pure table before the LORD,” renewed every sabbath, with the old loaves eaten by the priests in the holy place. The command concerning it is as plain as it is easy to pass over: “thou shalt set upon the table shewbread before me alway.” The Hebrew calls it the bread of the face — bread set before the presence of God. Its doctrine is covenantal rather than nutritional. The twelve cakes answer to the twelve tribes, so that the whole people stand continually represented before God in the holy place; alway and continual are the governing words; and the arrangement is one of fellowship, a table set and a meal shared in the house of God. The detail about the journey matters as well, for the table was carried covered but never emptied: the bread remained on it while Israel moved.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Shewbread, among the Jews, bread of exhibition; the twelve loaves placed on the golden table in the sanctuary, renewed every sabbath. The table of shewbread, Numbers 4:7, the table on which they were set.

Num 4:7 — "And upon the table of shewbread they shall spread a cloth of blue, and put thereon the dishes, and the spoons, and the bowls, and covers to cover withal: and the continual bread shall be thereon:"

Exo 25:23 — "Thou shalt also make a table of shittim wood: two cubits shall be the length thereof, and a cubit the breadth thereof, and a cubit and a half the height thereof."

Modern Corruption

The sanctuary furniture is treated as archaeological detail with no present claim, so that a table set continually before God — a picture of the people represented and fed in His presence — teaches nothing.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The neglect is the problem. Much modern reading treats the tabernacle chapters as inventory to be skimmed on the way to narrative, and a generation of Christians consequently cannot say what stood in the holy place or why. The loss is real, because the New Testament reasons from this furniture constantly and cannot be followed without it. Hebrews argues from the arrangement of the sanctuary; our Lord Himself appeals to the shewbread when the Pharisees charge His disciples with breaking the sabbath, reasoning from David eating the bread which was not lawful for him to eat.

The opposite error is over-reading, in which every dish and spoon is assigned a hidden meaning on no authority but the expositor's ingenuity, and the text becomes a code. Scripture's own emphases are the safe guide, and they are three: the bread is before the LORD, it is continual, and it is twelve. The people are represented, permanently, in the presence of God. That is a picture of intercession and of covenant memory, and it is answered in the New Testament by a High Priest who ever liveth to make intercession. The principle to recover is that the furniture preaches: a table set perpetually in God's house says that His people are kept before His face, and are fed there, and that neither the setting nor the feeding depends on their being in camp or on the march.
